newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech c.bank says leaves monetary policy unchanged.
newsitem.headline: Czech c.bank says leaves monetary policy unchanged.

text.p: The Czech central bank (CNB) on Thursday said it saw no reason to change the current course of its monetary policy, a CNB statement issued after a regular bank board meeting said.
The statement added that it would like to see an agreement between the government, labour officials and workers to limit wage growth in 1997 to a nominal 10 percent.

"On the basis of the latest results of the development of inflation, economic demand, GDP and the balance of payments the board stated the basic tendencies which caused the character of monetary policy in the second half of last year continue, and therefore create no objective reason for a change in policy," the statement said.

Last summer the central bank implemented a series of tightening measures -- including hiking rates and minimum reserve requirements -- to slow a burgeoning money supply and choke off inflationary tendencies.
The key discount rate currently stands at 10.5 percent.
The statement added that one of the main concerns of the CNB remains wage growth, which rose 14.4 percent, in year-on-year nominal terms in January.

"The board considers the main problem of the current (economic) development to be growth of wages, which is the main source of the growing gap between domestic supply and demand and therefore a high trade and current account deficit," the statement said.
"This worsens the conditions for keeping the crown stable," it added.

The Czech economy has enjoyed seven years of demand-led growth as industry imported technology and the population, which has seen its wages rise sharply over the past few years, satisfied its thirst for consumer goods.

However, some cracks have begun to appear with industrial output failing to keep pace with wages, and in fact weakening recently, indicating investment has not been effective and that industry has not carried out vital restructuring.
